title: Measuring & Plotting Lengths
keyIdea: To measure a length, line up one end of the object with 0 on the ruler, then read the mark at the other end. If the end falls between two marks, choose the whole centimetre it is closest to. To show many measurements at once, draw a line plot: a number line marked in equal steps of whole centimetres, with one X above the length of each object. Xs for the same length stack up.
familyTip: Collect about ten leaves, pencils or toy cars. Measure each one to the nearest centimetre and write the numbers down. Draw a number line with every whole centimetre from the shortest to the longest, then put one X above each length. Ask: which length came up most? How many are longer than 7 cm?

visual.caption: Is each measurement done right? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Leave out numbers with no Xs

lab.caption: Flagship lab: slide a leaf to 0, round three leaves to the nearest cm, plot ten lengths as Xs, read the plot and fix a broken scale.

kid: To measure how long something is, put one end at 0 on the ruler. Then look at the other end. The number there is the length. If you start at 2 instead, the end number is too big. A leaf from 2 to 9 is only 9 − 2 = 7 cm long.

Ends do not always land on a mark. Then you round to the nearest whole centimetre. Look at which mark the end is closer to. A leaf that ends at 6 and a little bit is about 6 cm. A leaf that ends nearly at 7 is about 7 cm.

A line plot shows lots of measurements at once. Draw a number line with every whole centimetre, in equal steps. Put one X above the length of each leaf. Two leaves that are both 6 cm get two Xs, one on top of the other, above 6.

Now you can read the plot. The tallest stack shows the most common length. The X furthest to the right is the longest leaf, and the one furthest to the left is the shortest. Keep every number on the line, even if it has no Xs.
adult: Ages 7 to 8. This matches Common Core grade 2, 2.MD.9: generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit, and show the measurements on a line plot whose horizontal scale is marked in whole-number units. In England it fits Year 2 measurement (choose and use units, measure length to the nearest cm) and statistics. Key words: length, centimetre, ruler, zero, nearest whole unit, data, line plot, scale, X mark, most common, longest, shortest.

A line plot (also called a dot plot) is a number line with a mark for each data value. In grade 2 the scale goes up in whole units, and each object gets exactly one X. Rounding to the nearest centimetre means choosing the nearer whole mark. In the lab, the rounded leaves are 4.8, 6.3 and 7.6 cm, so none sits exactly on a half.

Common mistakes: starting at 1 or at the end of the ruler and reading the end number as the length; always rounding up; drawing one X for a length instead of one per object; reading the numbers on the scale as counts; leaving out numbers with no Xs, so the steps are uneven; and mixing up the most common length with the longest.

In the lab your child slides a leaf from 2 to 0 and sees that 2 to 9 is 7 cm. They round three leaves, stack ten lengths as Xs, and read the plot to find the most common, longest and shortest lengths. Then they count the leaves longer than 7 cm and fix a scale that skipped 7.

practice.prompt: A crayon goes from 0 to 8 on a ruler. How long is it?
practice.hint: When one end is at 0, the number at the other end is the length.
practice.explain: It starts at 0 and ends at 8, so it is 8 cm long.

practice.prompt: A pencil starts at the {a} cm mark and ends at the {b} cm mark. How long is it in cm?
practice.hint: The length is the gap between the two marks: take the start away from the end.
practice.explain: {b} − {a} = {=b-a}, so the pencil is {=b-a} cm long.

practice.prompt: A shell ends just past 5, not near 6. To the nearest cm it is…
practice.hint: Which whole mark is the end closer to?
practice.explain: The end is much closer to the 5 mark than the 6 mark, so it is about 5 cm.

practice.prompt: A line plot has {x} Xs above 7 cm and 2 Xs above 8 cm. How many objects are 7 cm or 8 cm long?
practice.hint: Each X is one object. Add the Xs in both stacks.

practice.prompt: Three leaves are each 6 cm long. How should the line plot show them?
practice.hint: Each leaf gets its own X.
practice.explain: Every leaf gets one X, so three 6 cm leaves make a stack of 3 Xs above 6.

pool.prompt: Where should one end of the object go on the ruler?
choices: At the end of the ruler
pool.hint: Start at the very first mark, before 1.
pool.explain: Line one end up with 0. Then the number at the other end is the length.

pool.prompt: A twig ends close to 9, just before it. To the nearest cm it is…
pool.hint: Which mark is closer to the end of the twig?
pool.explain: The end is nearly at 9, so to the nearest whole centimetre it is 9 cm.

pool.prompt: On a line plot, what does each X stand for?
pool.hint: Count the Xs to count the objects.
pool.explain: Each X is one object, placed above its length.

pool.prompt: A ribbon starts at {s} cm and ends at {e} cm on a ruler. How long is it in cm?
pool.hint: Take the start mark away from the end mark to find the gap between them.
pool.explain: The length is the gap from start to end: {e} − {s} = {=e-s} cm.

pool.prompt: No leaf is 10 cm long. Should 10 still be on the line plot's scale?
choices: Yes, every whole number gets a place
pool.hint: A line plot is a number line with equal steps.
pool.explain: Keep every whole number, equally spaced, even ones with no Xs.

pool.prompt: The tallest stack of Xs is above 7. What does that tell you?
choices: 7 cm is the most common length
pool.hint: A tall stack means many objects had that length.
pool.explain: The tallest stack is the length that came up most often: 7 cm.

pool.prompt: A line plot has 1 X above 5, {a} Xs above 6 and 3 Xs above 7. How many objects were measured?
pool.hint: Each X is one object, so add up all the Xs on the plot.

pool.prompt: Sam's line plot goes 4, 5, 6, 8, 9. What is wrong?
choices: 7 is missing, so the steps are not equal
pool.hint: Count up in ones. Is any number skipped?
pool.explain: The scale skips 7. A line plot needs every whole number in equal steps.

pool.prompt: Which X on a line plot shows the shortest leaf?
choices: The one furthest to the left
The one at the top of the tallest stack
The one furthest to the right
pool.hint: Numbers on the line get bigger as you go right.
pool.explain: Smaller lengths are on the left, so the X furthest left is the shortest leaf.
